identity.title: WAVE: Learning Unified & Versatile Audio-Visual Embeddings with Multimodal LLM

problem.claim: Develop unified, versatile embeddings spanning text, audio, and video, supporting cross-modal retrieval and instruction-conditioned representations.

gap.claim: Although multimodal LLM embeddings are strong general-purpose representations, their use for dynamic audio and video modalities remains underexplored.

contributions.claim: WAVE combines hierarchical feature fusion with joint multimodal, multitask training to support any-to-any retrieval and prompt-aware embeddings.
The authors introduce a benchmark for versatile audio-visual learning and release code and checkpoints.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors describe WAVE as the first LLM-based embedding designed to create a unified representation space for text, audio, and video.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report state-of-the-art performance on the MMEB-v2 video benchmark and superior audio and video-to-audio retrieval results.
The authors report that prompt-aware WAVE embeddings significantly outperform existing embedding models on multimodal question answering.
The authors report ablations showing improved performance across all modalities from their joint training strategy.

narrative_sequence.summary: The paper identifies limited exploration of multimodal LLM embeddings for dynamic audio and video.
It introduces WAVE as a unified text-audio-video embedding and describes hierarchical fusion plus joint multimodal, multitask training.
The authors report gains on video benchmarking, audio/video-to-audio retrieval, and multimodal question answering.
Ablations are reported to support joint training; the authors also present a benchmark and release implementation artifacts.

source_observation.claim: The abstract links each major capability to an explicit design choice: hierarchical fusion and joint training are presented as enabling retrieval and prompt-aware embeddings.

lessons.interpretation: This makes the method narrative easier to evaluate because architectural choices are connected directly to intended functions.
lessons.application: When presenting a multimodal system, map each claimed capability to the mechanism intended to produce it, then test that mapping with targeted ablations.
lessons.exception: This framing is less suitable when the contribution is primarily a dataset, theoretical result, or an exploratory system without separable mechanisms.

unknowns: The abstract gives no metrics, dataset sizes, baseline identities, or detailed evaluation conditions for the reported comparisons.
The specific protocol and results for the newly introduced benchmark are not stated.
The ablation design and the meaning of improvement across all modalities are not quantified.
